title: Symphony No. 10 in E minor
hook: The first symphony after Stalin’s death, ending with the composer signing his own name in notes.

painting.title: Morning of the Streltsy Execution
painting.pairingNote: Peter the Great watches as the rebel guardsmen he condemned say farewell to their families; a Russian ruler’s terror seen through its victims, the shadow many listeners hear in this symphony.

facts: Stalin died on 5 March 1953. Shostakovich had written no symphony since his Ninth in 1945; three years later, in 1948, his music had been officially condemned. The Tenth was first played in Leningrad on 17 December 1953, by the Leningrad Philharmonic under Evgeny Mravinsky.
Shostakovich said he wrote it between July and October 1953, but some of its ideas are older: there are sketches from 1946, and one friend said it was finished in 1951.

In *Testimony*, a memoir published in 1979 by Solomon Volkov, Shostakovich is quoted as saying the violent second movement is a portrait of Stalin. The book’s authenticity is disputed, and nothing from 1953 confirms that reading.

What is certain is a personal code. In the third and fourth movements Shostakovich signs the music with his own initials as notes, the [[dsch|DSCH]] [[motif|motif]], and a horn call spells out the name of Elmira Nazirova, a young pianist and former pupil he was writing to at the time.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a long, dark meditation (I), four minutes of violence (II), a coded dance of two names (III), and a finale where the composer’s signature wins (IV).

movements.heading: Moderato
movements.summary: The longest movement, slow and brooding. It grows from a quiet phrase in the low strings into an enormous climax and sinks back again. Two lonely woodwind melodies, one on the clarinet and one on the flute, carry most of the musical thought. It is in a free [[sonata-form|sonata form]].

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: a slow, winding phrase in cellos and basses, quiet and grave.

mainIdeas.name: The flute’s tune
mainIdeas.description: a hesitant little dance, a kind of sad [[waltz|waltz]].

stops.hear: Cellos and basses alone, very low and quiet: a slow, winding phrase
The violins take up the phrase, high and thin; the music stays hushed
stops.happening: The opening idea spreads through the strings

stops.hear: A solo clarinet begins a long, sad, wandering melody
The melody grows; more instruments join and the strings rise to a first, aching peak
A solo flute plays a hesitant, limping little dance over plucked strings
stops.happening: The second theme, a sad waltz

stops.hear: The low opening phrase returns, and the music slowly gathers weight
A long, relentless build: brass, timpani and the whole orchestra, louder and louder
stops.happening: The great climax of the movement

stops.hear: The storm breaks off; the music is left shaken and quiet
The sad little dance returns in the woodwinds, quieter and more fragile

stops.label: Last two minutes
stops.hear: Two piccolos play a thin, high duet over a low, held note; the music fades away

notice: The movement’s loudest point comes after about a quarter of an hour of slow growth. Listen to how gradually the tension rises.
The ending is given to the highest instruments in the orchestra, two piccolos, with almost nothing in between them and the bass.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Karajan conducted this symphony for Shostakovich in Moscow in May 1969, on a Berlin Philharmonic tour, and the composer came on stage at the end. This is the second of his two studio recordings of it, made in Berlin in February 1981.

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: Four minutes of relentless speed and violence. Short, stabbing phrases, rushing strings and pounding drums never let up. It is the movement that *Testimony* calls a portrait of Stalin.

mainIdeas.name: The rush
mainIdeas.description: fast strings in a hammering rhythm, with a snare drum driving it on.

mainIdeas.name: The shrieks
mainIdeas.description: piercing, off-beat cries in the woodwinds and brass.

stops.hear: Strings attack at full speed with short, hard chords
The woodwinds shriek a sharp, jagged tune
The snare drum rattles; brass join in
Everything at full force, brass blaring over the rushing strings

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A final burst and a sudden stop
stops.happening: The movement ends as abruptly as it began

notice: There is hardly a quiet bar in the whole movement. Notice how the shortest movement feels the most crushing.

movements.heading: Allegretto
movements.summary: A strange, wry dance, part waltz, part nocturne. Two four- and five-note codes run through it: Shostakovich’s own initials, DSCH, and a horn call that spells the name Elmira. They take turns, as in a conversation, until the end.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, slightly mechanical tune in the strings.

mainIdeas.name: DSCH
mainIdeas.description: four notes, D, E-flat, C, B, often in the woodwinds. Shostakovich’s signature.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: five notes, E, A, E, D, A, played twelve times by a solo horn. In note names it spells “E-La-Mi-Re-A”, Elmira.

stops.hear: The strings play a quiet, slightly stiff dance tune
stops.happening: The opening dance, in C minor

stops.hear: The woodwinds play a short, four-note phrase, repeated and turned around
A solo horn calls out five notes, slow and far away, over a hush
The dance and the horn call alternate; the horn returns again and again
The music grows louder and harsher; DSCH is hammered out
Quiet again; the horn call returns, answered by DSCH in the woodwinds

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: A flute and piccolo play DSCH very softly; the horn sounds its call one last time

notice: Count the horn calls. There are twelve, always the same five notes.
Listen for who answers whom. When the horn has called, the woodwinds often reply with DSCH.

movements.heading: Andante – Allegro
movements.summary: A slow introduction with long, lonely woodwind solos, then a fast, light-footed dance that slowly gathers energy. At its height the whole orchestra hammers out DSCH. After a quiet, uncertain passage the fast music returns, and the symphony ends in E major with the timpani pounding the composer’s signature.

mainIdeas.name: The introduction
mainIdeas.description: long solos on oboe, flute and bassoon over low strings.

mainIdeas.name: The Allegro
mainIdeas.description: a quick, almost cheerful dance tune in the violins.

mainIdeas.name: DSCH
mainIdeas.description: now in the full orchestra and, at the end, on the timpani.

stops.hear: Low strings, very slow and quiet
A solo oboe plays a long, lonely, searching melody
The flute and then the bassoon take up long solos
Suddenly quick and light: the violins play a skipping dance tune
The dance gathers speed and weight, spreading through the orchestra
The full orchestra hammers out a four-note phrase, with a crash
stops.happening: DSCH at full force. The climax

stops.hear: Quiet and unsettled; a bassoon plays the dance tune slowly and awkwardly
The fast dance returns and races on

stops.label: Last two minutes
stops.hear: The timpani pound out four notes again and again; the orchestra ends loudly in E major
stops.happening: DSCH on the timpani. The composer’s signature has the last word

notice: Listen for the four-note signature in the timpani near the end. The same notes appeared quietly in the third movement.
The finale’s dance tune sounds cheerful. Ask yourself whether it stays cheerful when DSCH breaks in.

threads.title: A signature
threads.body: The DSCH motif runs through the second half of the symphony and closes it. Shostakovich used it again in later works, most famously the String Quartet No. 8 (1960).

threads.title: Two names
threads.body: In the third movement Shostakovich’s name and Elmira Nazirova’s horn call alternate like a dialogue. In letters to her he described the horn call himself.

threads.title: Dark to light
threads.body: The symphony starts in the low strings in E minor and ends in E major. Whether the ending is victory or defiance is for the listener to decide.

threads.title: After Stalin
threads.body: Whatever its private story, the Tenth was the first symphony Shostakovich released after Stalin’s death, and its premiere was followed by a long public debate in the Composers’ Union about whether it was too gloomy.
